No. Honest assessment: It was unfair to young people.

- **Generational burden**: AHV is already an intergenerational transfer system (working-age taxpayers fund retirees). Adding a 13th pillar during a low-growth, inflationary environment compounded the relative burden on those starting their careers or paying off education/debt.

- **Timing & opportunity cost**: Approved in 2024, so the cost (and taxes/insurances the 22-year-old will pay long-term) hits exactly the cohort beginning their working lives when they have the fewest resources and politicians have promised them the least future security.

- **Long-term planning**: It reduces projected private-savings capacity because of higher mandatory contributions and lower real wages/social benefits earlier in careers.

- **Political optics vs. economics**: It may make policymakers feel popular in the short term, but economically it skews transfer weights toward retirees while squeezing the starting capital of the next generation.

So, viewed through either fiscal fairness or inter-generational equity lenses, it leans heavily against fairness to today’s young adults.
